title: Random variables and distributions
summary: A random variable attaches a number to each outcome of an uncertain process; its distribution says how one unit of probability is shared among the values. Samples are what we actually see, and their histogram settles onto the distribution as the count grows.
llm_link: At every step a language model outputs a probability distribution over its whole vocabulary, and generating text means sampling one token from it. That is why the same prompt can give different continuations.
key_ideas: A random variable X is a function: outcome in, number out (a die roll maps a face to 1-6).
A discrete distribution gives p(x) for every value, with every p(x) >= 0 and the sum of p(x) equal to 1.
Samples are draws from the distribution. The fraction of samples equal to x approaches p(x) as the number of samples grows (law of large numbers).
Continuous quantities have a density p(x): probability is the area under the curve between a and b, and the total area is 1. The height at one point is not a probability.

quiz.q: Which of these lists can be a probability distribution over four values?
quiz.explain: Every entry must be at least 0 and the entries must add up to exactly 1. Only [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4] does both; [0.6, 0.6, −0.2, 0] sums to 1 but has a negative entry.

quiz.q: A loaded die has p(6) = 0.5 and p = 0.1 for each other face. Predict the result: roughly how many sixes in 1,000 rolls?
quiz.explain: The fraction of sixes settles near p(6) = 0.5, so about 500. It will rarely be exactly 500: samples wobble around the true value.

quiz.q: Why is a random variable better described as a function than as a variable?
options: Because it maps each outcome of the uncertain process to a number
Because it is always between 0 and 1
Because it is the same thing as its distribution
quiz.explain: X takes an outcome (a face of the die, a person, a moment) and returns a number. Its distribution is a separate object: how probability is spread over those numbers.

quiz.q: For a continuous height distribution, what does the area under the density between 165 cm and 176 cm give you?
options: The probability that a height falls between 165 and 176 cm
Nothing: only heights at a single point matter
quiz.explain: With a density, probability is area. The probability of any one exact height is zero; intervals carry the probability.

quiz.q: A language model gives the next token p(mat) = 0.46, p(floor) = 0.22 and spreads the rest over other tokens. You generate twice from the same prompt. What should you expect?
options: Always "mat", because it has the largest probability
Possibly different tokens, because generation samples from the distribution
An error, because probabilities must be 0 or 1
quiz.explain: Sampling draws "mat" about 46% of the time, not every time. Always taking the top token is a different strategy (greedy decoding).

problems.title: Is it a distribution?
problems.prompt:
Write is_distribution(p) that returns True if the list p is a valid discrete probability distribution and False otherwise.

Valid means: every entry is at least 0, and the entries add up to 1. Floating-point sums are rarely exact (0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004), so accept a sum within 1e-9 of 1.

is_distribution([0.5, 0.5])        # True
is_distribution([0.6, 0.6, -0.2])  # False (negative entry)
is_distribution([0.3, 0.3])        # False (sums to 0.6)

tests.name: accepts a fair coin
tests.code: assert is_distribution([0.5, 0.5]) is True, 'a fair coin [0.5, 0.5] is a valid distribution: no negatives and it sums to 1'

tests.name: tolerates floating-point sums
tests.code: assert is_distribution([0.1, 0.2, 0.7]) is True, '0.1 + 0.2 + 0.7 is not exactly 1.0 in floating point; compare abs(sum(p) - 1) < 1e-9 instead of sum(p) == 1'

tests.name: rejects negative entries
tests.code: assert is_distribution([0.6, 0.6, -0.2]) is False, '[0.6, 0.6, -0.2] sums to 1 but a probability can never be negative; check every entry'

tests.name: rejects a wrong total
tests.code: assert is_distribution([0.3, 0.3]) is False, 'the entries must add up to 1; [0.3, 0.3] only adds up to 0.6'

tests.name: loaded die is fine
tests.code: assert is_distribution([0.1]*5 + [0.5]) is True, 'the loaded die [0.1]*5 + [0.5] sums to 1 with no negatives, so it is valid'

hints: any(x < 0 for x in p) tells you whether some entry is negative.

problems.title: Sample from a distribution
problems.prompt:
Computers give us uniform random numbers u between 0 and 1. To turn one into a draw from a distribution p, lay the probabilities end to end along [0, 1] and see which piece u lands in: the first value owns [0, p[0]), the second owns [p[0], p[0]+p[1]), and so on.

Write sample(p, u) that returns the index of the piece containing u.

p = [0.2, 0.5, 0.3]
sample(p, 0.10)   # 0   (0.10 < 0.2)
sample(p, 0.65)   # 1   (0.2 <= 0.65 < 0.7)
sample(p, 0.95)   # 2

Then use it with random.random() many times and count: the fractions should approach p.
problems.starter:
def sample(p, u):
    # TODO: walk through p keeping a running total.
    #       As soon as u < running total, return the current index.
    total = 0

    return len(p) - 1  # fallback for u extremely close to 1

tests.name: first piece
tests.code:
out = sample([0.2, 0.5, 0.3], 0.10)
assert out == 0, f'u = 0.10 lies in [0, 0.2), which belongs to index 0; got {out}'

tests.name: middle piece
tests.code:
out = sample([0.2, 0.5, 0.3], 0.65)
assert out == 1, f'u = 0.65 lies in [0.2, 0.7), which belongs to index 1; got {out}. Are you comparing u with the running total rather than with p[i] alone?'

tests.name: last piece
tests.code:
out = sample([0.2, 0.5, 0.3], 0.95)
assert out == 2, f'u = 0.95 lies in [0.7, 1.0), index 2; got {out}'

tests.name: boundary goes to the next piece
tests.code:
out = sample([0.5, 0.5], 0.5)
assert out == 1, f'pieces are half-open: [0, 0.5) is index 0 and [0.5, 1) is index 1, so u = 0.5 gives 1; got {out}. Use u < total, not u <= total'

tests.name: frequencies approach p
tests.code:
import random
random.seed(0)
p = [0.1]*5 + [0.5]
N = 20000
c = [0]*6
for _ in range(N):
    c[sample(p, random.random())] += 1
f = [x / N for x in c]
assert abs(f[5] - 0.5) < 0.02, f'with 20000 draws the fraction of index 5 should be close to 0.5, got {f[5]:.3f}; check that each value owns a piece as wide as its probability'

hints: for i, pi in enumerate(p): total += pi, then check u < total.
The pieces are cumulative sums: 0.2, then 0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7, then 1.0.

out = frequencies(np.array([1, 1]))
assert out.shape == (6,), f'expected shape (6,) even when high faces never appear, got {out.shape}; pass minlength=6 to np.bincount'

tests.name: fractions sum to 1
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out = frequencies(np.array([2, 3, 3, 5, 6]))
assert abs(out.sum() - 1) < 1e-9, f'fractions of all rolls must add up to 1, got {out.sum()}; divide counts by len(rolls)'

tests.name: law of large numbers
tests.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rolls = rng.choice(np.arange(1, 7), size=50000, p=[0.1]*5 + [0.5])
out = frequencies(rolls)
assert np.allclose(out, [0.1]*5 + [0.5], atol=0.01), f'with 50000 rolls the fractions should be within 0.01 of the true probabilities, got {np.round(out, 3)}'

hints: rolls - 1 shifts faces 1..6 to indices 0..5 for every element at once (broadcasting a scalar).
